title: Lifted Causal Inference in Relational Domains
authors: Malte Luttermann, Mattis Hartwig, Tanya Braun, Ralf MÃ¶ller, Marcel Gehrke
text:
A fundamental problem in the research field of artificial intelligence for an intelligent agent is to plan and act rationally in a relational domain. To compute the best possible action in a perceived state, the agent considers the available actions and chooses the one with the maximum expected utility. When computing the expected utility of an action that acts on a specific variable, it is crucial to deploy the semantics of an intervention instead of a typical conditioning on that variable [1]. When calculating the effect of an intervention, a specific variable is set to a fixed value and all incoming probabilistic causal influences of this variable must be ignored for the specific query. It is therefore fundamental to deploy the semantics of an intervention instead of the typical conditioning to correctly determine the effect of an action.

Over the last years, causal graphical models have become a widely used formalism to answer questions concerning the causal impact of a treatment variable on an outcome variable. These models combine probabilistic modeling with causal knowledge, which enables computing the effect of an action that intervenes on a particular variable. As our world is inherently relational (i.e., it consists of objects and relations between those objects), it is particularly important to have models that represent the relational structure between objects in addition to capturing causal knowledge. However, commonly applied causal graphical models focus on propositional representations while at the same time relational models lack the ability to efficiently apply causal knowledge for inference. Therefore, we aim to combine the best of both worlds to allow for efficient causal inference in relational domains. In particular, this paper deals with the problem of efficiently computing causal effects in models representing objects and their causal relationships to each other.

## Previous work.

To perform causal effect estimation in causal graphical models, there has been a considerable amount of work and most of this work focuses on models of propositional data [2,1]. Some works extend propositional fg by adding edge directions to enable the computation of the effect of interventions [3,4]. [5] show that propositional models are insufficient to represent causal relationships within relational domains as required by real-world applications. To express causal dependencies within relational domains, [6] introduce so-called rcm but focus on learning rcm from observed data. Further related work covering rcm also focuses on causal discovery and reasoning about conditional independence (e.g., [7,8,9]). \Acp rcm have also been extended to cover cyclic dependency structures [10,11], however, both non-cyclic and cyclic rcm allow only for reasoning about conditional independence on a lifted level but they do not allow for lifted causal inference. Prior work dealing with the estimation of causal effects in relational domains applies propositional probabilistic inference [12,13] and thus does not scale for large graphs. Consequently, there is a lack of efficient algorithms to compute causal effects in relational domains. In probabilistic inference, lifting exploits symmetries in a relational model, allowing to carry out query answering more efficiently while maintaining exact answers [14]. First introduced by [15], pfg and lve (lve) allow to perform lifted probabilistic inference, i.e., to exploit symmetries in a probabilistic graphical model, resulting in significant speed-ups for probabilistic query answering in relational domains. Over time, lve has been refined by many researchers to reach its current form [16,17,18,19,20,21]. \Acp pfg are well-studied for many years and have been developed further to efficiently perform probabilistic inference not only for single queries but also for sets of queries [22], to incorporate probabilistic inference over time [23,24], and, among other extensions, to allow for decision making by following the maximum expected utility principle [25,26,27]. Markov logic networks are another lifted representation and have been extended to incorporate maximum expected utility as well [28]. Nevertheless, when a decision-making agent plans for the best action to take, previous works improperly apply conditioning (i.e., actions are treated as evidence), as also suggested by [29], instead of the notion of an intervention. Treating actions as evidence, however, is incorrect as noted by [1]. To correctly handle the semantics of an action, the notion of an intervention [30] has to be applied. Therefore, in this paper, we close the gap between pfg and causal inference in relational domains by introducing pcfg as an extension of pfg incorporating causal knowledge to allow for lifted causal inference, thereby enabling efficient decision making using the notion of an intervention.

## Our contributions.

pfg are well-established models coming with lve as a mature lifted inference algorithm, allowing for tractable probabilistic inference with respect to domain sizes in relational domains. We extend pfg by incorporating causal knowledge, resulting in pcfg for which we define a formal semantics of interventions. Having defined a formal semantics of interventions in pcfg, we show how causal effects can be efficiently computed, even for multiple simultaneous interventions. We further introduce the lci (lci) algorithm that operates on a lifted level to allow for lifted causal inference in relational domains. Apart from the theoretical investigation of pcfg and the lci algorithm, we provide an empirical evaluation confirming the efficiency of lci.

## Structure of this paper.

In Section 2, we introduce both fg and pfg as undirected probabilistic graphical models. Thereafter, in Section 3, we define pcfg as an extension of pfg incorporating causal knowledge and provide a formal semantics of interventions in pcfg. In Section 4, we introduce the lci algorithm operating on a pcfg and show how lci computes causal effects on a lifted level to avoid grounding the pcfg as much as possible. Afterwards, in our empirical evaluation in Section 5, we investigate the speed-up of lci compared to performing propositional causal inference both in causal bn and in directed fg before we conclude in Section 6.
